newsitem.title: USA: Mercantile buys Mark Twain, combining St. Louis banks.
newsitem.headline: Mercantile buys Mark Twain, combining St. Louis banks.

text.p: Mercantile Bancorp Inc., moving to expand its role in the Missouri banking market, said Monday it agreed to buy Mark Twain Bancshares Inc., another St. Louis bank holding company, in a deal valued at $855 million.

The addition of Mark Twain, with $3.1 billion in assets, and its 39 locations in the St. Louis and Kansas City, Mo., areas will strengthen Mercantile's presence in the three largest Missouri markets. Mercantile has $18.2 billion in assets.

"It's an in-market deal, which allows for a tremendous ammount of efficiencies, which is good for Mercantile," said Joseph Steiven, an analyst at Stifel Nicolaus. "They're paying full-boat prices, but they're getting an excellent company."
Under the terms of the agreement, Mark Twain shareholders will receive 0.9520 share of Mercantile common stock for each share of Mark Twain common, the banks said.

Based on Friday's closing price of $52.125 for Mercantile's common stock, the deal is valued at $49.62 per share of Mark Twain, they said. The transaction was structured as a merger through a tax-free exchange of shares, they said.
The deal comes two months after NationsBank Corp. said it would acquire St. Louis-based Boatmen's Bancshares Inc. in a deal valued at about $9.5 billion.
"It's a pretty pricey transaction," said James Schutz, banking analyst at Chicago Corp. "The question I would ask is, 'How is Mercantile going to earn back this premium they're paying?'"
That question also appeared to be in the stock market. Mark Twain's shares jumped $3.625 to $46, while Mercantile fell $2 to $50, both on the New York Stock Exchange.

Mark Twain Chief Executive John Dubinsky, who will become chief executive of Mercantile's largest bank, Mercantile Bank of St. Louis, indicated widespread job cuts will not be used to pay for the deal.

"Between Mercantile and Mark Twain as we sit here today, there are over 200 job openings," Dubinsky said in an interview. "There will be some duplications, there will be some consolidation of job functions." But "quality" individuals whose jobs are eliminated because of duplicaiton will be able to apply for other jobs, he said.
"I would be very surprised if there was a large number of individuals that won't be needed," he added.
Upon completion of the merger, Alvin Siteman, chairman of Mark Twain Bancshares, will become chairman of Mercantile Bank of St. Louis and join the Mercantile Bancorp board.
Dubinsky will also become a member of Mercantile's management executive committee.
Both men will report to Mercantile Bancorp Chairman and Chief Executive Thomas Jacobsen.

Mercantile Bancorp operates banks in Missouri, Iowa, Kansas, Illinois and Arkansas. Its non-banking subsidiaries include companies providing brokerage services, asset-based lending, investment advisory services, leasing services and credit life insurance.

"This merger ... brings together the strengths of two high-performing organisations and solidifies Mercantile's position as the largest locally managed, and independently owned banking operation in St. Louis and the state of Missouri," Jacobsen said in a statement announcing the agreement.
Plans call for the merger to be completed in the second quarter of 1997, subject to the approval of Mercantile and Mark Twain shareholders and all appropriate regulatory agencies, the companies said.
Mercantile also has mergers pending with Today's Bancorp, Inc., First Financial Corp. of America, and Regional Bancshares Inc.
